Public Hearings:
Continuation of the Public Hearing, recessed from the December 1, 2021 meeting,

Mr. Hyde explained that, since the December meeting, a working group consisting of Dave Evans (Farm Bureau), Chet Hansen (Dairy Operator), Conley Moon (Cattleman), Troy Cooper (USU Extension), Darrell Gillman (NRCS), Tracy Killian (Feed Lot Operator), Tom Henderson (Cattleman) and Malarik Harrison (Dairy Operator) met with county staff to amend the draft Large CAFO overlay zone map and ordinance in a manner that could be supported by the agriculture industry.  Mr. Hyde noted that the recommendation of the working group was to expand the Large CAFO area to include all of the Pleasant Valley area to the Uintah County line and to establish an overlay zone in the Arcadia area, around 4-C Farms.  The ordinance text has been amended to remove the requirement for anaerobic digesters as those would be considered as part of the Comprehensive Nutrient Management Plan.  It has been indicated that anaerobic digesters are not effective in colder climates like the Uintah Basin.  The text has been amended to clarify that a change in ownership or operator of a Large CAFO would not affect the land use status of the facility, provided that it continues to be operated in accordance with state and federal requirements.  The text has been amended to clarify that an existing Large CAFO located outside of the overlay zone boundary would be allowed to expand in terms of acreage covered and in the number of animals.  There was discussion about not allowing the species of animals to change during an expansion; but the working group felt that producers should be allowed to change species, if necessary, due to changing market conditions.  The text has been amended to clarify that an existing Animal Feeding Operation could expand into Large CAFO status, even though located outside of the overlay zone, but within an A-5 or A-10 agricultural zone, provided that a Comprehensive Nutrient Management Plan has been approved and all other state and federal regulations have been met.  Mr. Hyde asked if there were any questions of the staff report.  As there were no questions of the staff, Chairman Sorensen called for those wishing to speak to the revised ordinance.  Charlie Hansen spoke and called on the County to not impose unnecessary restrictions on the agriculture industry.  He has an approved nutrient management plan and agreed that anaerobic digesters do not work well in Utah.  Tracy Killian spoke and recommended that the County restrict housing developments from encroaching near agricultural uses to help reduce conflicts.  The USDA adequately regulates Large CAFOs.  Mr. Hyde noted that ?Right to Farm? laws help protect agricultural uses from encroaching residential development.  Also, agricultural protection zones can be formed to further protect agricultural operations.  Shane Rowley expressed support for the proposed ordinance based on the recommendations of the working group.  Dave Evans noted that the agricultural industry is fairly stable and helps the County withstand the ups and downs of the energy industry.  He encouraged the County to not

impose restrictions on agriculture that would be detrimental to the operators and their ability to produce the food that we need.  Tom Henderson spoke and agreed with the proposed ordinance.  He felt that the approval of a nutrient management plan should address most concerns.  Keith Hicken spoke and inquired if establishment of the Large CAFO overlay zone would affect the ability to locate businesses, like the ?Speedy Goat? store, in the Pleasant Valley area.  Mr. Hyde verified that it would not.  Tracy Killian and Dave Evans re-stated their desire that the Planning Commission recommend the proposed ordinance to the County Commissioners.  After the conclusion of testimony, Chairman Sorensen closed the public hearing.  There was discussion by the Commissioners whether to amend the proposed ordinance to limit the expansion of existing animal feeding operations to require such expansion to occur either adjacent to or within a certain distance of the existing operation.  Commissioner Drake made a motion and amended it several times to require such expansion to be adjacent, within ? mile, ? mile or within one mile of an existing operation.  The motion and its amendments were not seconded.  Commissioner Giles made a motion to recommend to the County Commissioners the approval of Ordinance #22-392 as recommended by staff and the working group.  Commissioner Sweat seconded the motion and it passed 4-1, with Commissioner Drake opposed.  Mr. Hyde noted that the County Commission is scheduled to open their public hearing on the proposal on January 10, 2022 at 1:30 PM. Mr. Hyde explained that, as a result of controversy associated with the expansion of hog farming operations in Millard County, the state legislature passed a bill in the 2021 general session to require counties wishing to regulate the location and operation of Large Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations (CAFOs) to pass an ordinance and establish at least one mapped area where they could be located, by February 1, 2022.  Mr. Hyde indicated the number of animals of varying species being fed that reach the threshold of a Large CAFO.  Examples of existing Large CAFOs in the County are the Fitzgerald, 4C Farms and Harvey dairies in the Bridgeland, Arcadia and Pleasant Valley areas respectively.  Mr. Gottfredson explained that the current county ordinance requires a 10,000-foot setback from incorporated towns, platted subdivisions, public or private water wells, public springs, public water intakes and a setback of 1,000 feet from property lines.  A GIS analysis revealed that the current code would prohibit new Large CAFOs in most areas of the county, with a few exceptions, which were displayed on a map.  Mr. Gottfredson noted that the County has been in contact with other counties in the state as they wrestle with this requirement.  We have heard that hog farms are the main issue and that their odors can travel 8 to 11 miles in some circumstances.  The area being proposed for Large CAFOs in Duchesne County is located south of Bridgeland, extending from west of Antelope Creek easterly toward the Pleasant Valley area.  The proposed Uinta Basin railway would be located in this area, which could be beneficial to a Large CAFO.  Mr. Hyde presented the staff report, indicating how the proposal complies with the criteria for zoning map and text amendments and recommended that the Planning Commission recommend to the County Commissioners the approval of Ordinance #21-390.  As there were no questions of the staff, Chairman Sorensen called for those wishing to speak to the proposed ordinance.  He asked that testimony be limited to 5 minutes due to the large number of attendees wishing to speak.  Shane Rowley, representing the Duchesne County Farm Bureau, spoke.  He questioned the designation of only one area.  He felt that areas such as western Arcadia, the Koch Field, Talmage and the Blue Bench could be considered.  Areas east of Neola are probably not suitable due to the Roosevelt City water source.  Mr. Rowley also spoke of the issues that farmers face as more residential development occurs and that farming operations need to be protected from complaints.

Mr. Hyde noted that there are ?Right to Farm? laws and tools such as Agricultural Protection Zones that can be used to address the incompatibility issues.  Tracy Killian spoke; noting that he has close to 1,000 head of cattle and that residential development south of Roosevelt keeps getting closer.  He is concerned whether this proposed ordinance would affect his operation.  Mr. Hyde indicated that the proposed ordinance would regulate new Large CAFOs; not existing ones.  Commissioner Wells inquired what other counties are doing and could they establish operations near the border that could affect Duchesne County?  Mr. Gottfredson noted that there was a cross-jurisdictional problem at the boundary between Garfield and Piute counties.  A Large CAFO was permitted in Garfield County, located about 500 feet away from the town of Circleville in Piute County.  Mr. Hyde noted that our neighboring counties are considering this issue as well and that any CAFOs in Uintah County would be downwind from Duchesne County; given the prevailing winds.  Brandon Hartman spoke; questioning whether existing animal feeding operations would be able to expand into Large CAFO status if they are located outside of the proposed map area?  The County should not prevent local cattlemen from growing their herds.  Mr. Hyde replied that the proposed ordinance is intended for new Large CAFOs, with feeding occurring at one location as opposed to operations that may have feeding locations spread across several parcels.  Brandon Bench spoke, indicating that the proposed CAFO area is not an area with potential to grow feed and not an area with existing fields that manure could be applied to.  Dustin Lemon spoke and suggested that the ordinance clarify whether change in ownership or operator would jeopardize the grandfathered status of an existing Large CAFO.  Dave Evans spoke and stressed the need of operators to grow to stay solvent and to feed a growing population.  Darrell Gillman spoke and noted that the NRCS no longer recommends the use of anaerobic digesters in many instances.  He encouraged the Commission to table the matter to allow a work group to meet and discuss amending the ordinance and map to address the questions raised tonight.  Chairman Sorensen called for discussion and inquired who among the attendees would be willing to serve on a working group.  The following individuals were appointed to the working group:  Dave Evans, Chet Hansen, Conley Moon, Troy Cooper, Darrell Gillman, Tracy Killian, Tom Henderson and Mali Harrison.  Commissioner Wells made a motion to recess this public hearing until January 5, 2021 to allow time for the working group to meet and make recommendations.  Commissioner Sweat seconded the motion and it passed unanimously.

Caller reported a release from the Rust 1-4B3 SWD Transfer station and noticed water running out of the valve set building on the 8 inch line. An estimated 130 bbls of produced water traveled 10? x 686? long northeast out of the valve set into a grass field. The release entered a small irrigation ditch with some free standing irrigation water then fanned out into the field. The release occurred due to a cracked 0.5-inch nipple under a pressure transducer on the 8-inch line. It appears that vibration from the 3-inch discharge line leaving the SWD Transfer station caused the nipple to crack, the nipple has been removed and the pressure transducer was left out of service for tonight. Approximately 3 bbls of produced water was recovered from puddles in the field. A clean-up of the visually impacted areas (i.e. iron sulfide) will be performed and removed from the site.
